name: Belief Perseverance
statement: People tend to keep holding a belief even after the evidence that originally supported it has been thoroughly discredited.
statementAccent: keep holding a belief even after the evidence that originally supported it has been thoroughly discredited
meaning: Belief perseverance, also called conceptual conservatism, is the tendency for an initial belief to survive largely intact even when the information that produced it is later shown to be false. It demonstrates that debunking the evidence behind a belief is often insufficient to remove the belief itself.
mechanism: A major driver is that people generate causal explanations for why a belief might be true, and those self-generated explanations continue to support the belief independently of the original evidence, even after that evidence is discredited. Cognitive-dissonance reduction and a general need for cognitive continuity also contribute to resistance against belief revision.

examples.text: In a 1975 study by Ross, Lepper, and Hubbard, subjects falsely told they had done well or poorly on a social-sensitivity test retained biased self-perceptions in the direction of the false feedback even after being fully debriefed that it was fabricated and random.
Ross and Anderson led subjects to falsely believe a firefighter’s stated risk preference predicted job performance; after debriefing revealed no such correlation, the induced beliefs persisted.

Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter’s 1956 study of a group predicting a flood before dawn on 21 December 1954 found that when the flood failed to occur, the most committed members did not abandon the belief but increased their devotion and proselytising.

whyItMatters: Belief perseverance explains why corrections, retractions, and fact-checks often fail to change minds, with direct implications for combating misinformation, improving jury and eyewitness reasoning, and designing effective debriefing procedures in research and education.
limits: The effect is not absolute — belief change does occur, particularly when people are prompted to generate explanations for the opposite outcome or when social commitment is low; Festinger et al. found less-committed members did abandon their belief after disconfirmation, while highly committed ones did not.
misreadings: It is often loosely equated with simple stubbornness or confirmation bias, but belief perseverance specifically concerns the survival of a belief after its originating evidential basis has been explicitly and credibly discredited, not merely a preference for confirming new evidence.
origin: The classic experimental demonstration is Ross, Lepper, and Hubbard’s 1975 debriefing-paradigm study; the phenomenon was developed further by Lee Ross and Craig A. Anderson and traces conceptually to Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter’s 1956 study of a doomsday group.
